stories.headline: Comcast to Spin Off NBCUniversal in Major Media Restructuring
stories.summary:
Comcast announced Monday it will spin off its NBCUniversal assets into a separate publicly traded company, one of the largest restructurings in American media in years. The spinoff would separate Comcast's broadband, wireless, and cable entertainment operations from NBCUniversal's broadcast and film properties, including NBC, Telemundo, Universal Pictures, Peacock, and Bravo.

Under the plan, existing Comcast shareholders would receive shares in both the new NBCUniversal entity and the restructured Comcast company. The move follows a broader trend of media conglomerates separating legacy broadcast and content assets from more stable and profitable infrastructure businesses such as internet and wireless services.

The decision reflects mounting pressure on traditional media companies as streaming competition intensifies, advertising revenue from linear television declines, and broadband infrastructure becomes the more reliable growth engine. NBCUniversal has faced particular challenges scaling Peacock against dominant rivals such as Netflix and Disney+.

stories.headline: Update: Paris Mortuaries Overwhelmed as France's Heat Wave Death Toll Mounts
stories.summary:
France's ongoing record-breaking heat wave has overwhelmed funeral homes and morgues in Paris and surrounding regions, with mortuary directors reporting cold storage facilities completely full and hundreds of unanswered calls from grieving families seeking space for the dead. Public Health France confirmed that deaths surged to more than 1,200 on the heat wave's peak day last Wednesday, rising to more than 1,400 on each of the two following days — roughly 50 percent above France's typical daily death rate of 900 to 1,000.

The national public health agency's preliminary estimate of at least 1,000 additional deaths during the three-day peak is expected to rise significantly as more death certificates are registered in coming weeks. The toll falls disproportionately on elderly people living alone at home, particularly in the Paris region. A rapid study by the World Weather Attribution scientific consortium found the heat would have been virtually impossible five decades ago and is now 200 times more likely than it was 20 years ago due to climate change.

As France begins tallying its human cost, the heat wave has moved eastward. Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic all set all-time temperature records over the weekend, with the Czech Republic reaching 41.9 degrees Celsius (107.4 Fahrenheit). The World Health Organization warned that Europe is now the fastest-warming continent and called for stronger measures to protect citizens from extreme heat.

stories.headline: NBA Player Malik Beasley Indicted on Federal Charges for Allegedly Fixing His Own Performances
stories.summary:
Former NBA guard Malik Beasley has been indicted on federal charges by a grand jury in the Eastern District of New York, accused of intentionally altering his on-court performance to benefit sports bettors in an alleged scheme that prosecutors say ran from December 2023 through April 2024. Beasley played for the Milwaukee Bucks during the period covered by the indictment.

Also charged are former NBA player Ed Davis, current player agent Paolo Zamorano, and three other men. The indictment includes counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, sports bribery, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, and money laundering conspiracy. Prosecutors allege Beasley communicated his intended underperformance to co-conspirators, who then placed wagers on his statistical prop bet lines in specific games, including matchups against Cleveland, Charlotte, and the Los Angeles Clippers.

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said the scheme "erodes the integrity of American sports and victimizes the sports-watching public." Four defendants were arrested Monday morning and are set for arraignment in Brooklyn. Beasley and Zamorano were not in custody as of Monday; Beasley's attorney said his client would arrange a voluntary surrender this week.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Peace Talks Resume Tuesday in Qatar as Both Sides Halt Weekend Strikes
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Monday that the United States and Iran will hold a new round of peace talks Tuesday in Doha, Qatar, after both sides agreed to halt a series of tit-for-tat attacks over the weekend that had threatened to collapse the fragile 60-day ceasefire framework. Trump said on Truth Social that Iran had requested the meeting, though Iranian officials had not publicly confirmed participation as of Monday. The weekend exchanges included fresh U.S. strikes and Iranian attacks on targets in Bahrain and Kuwait.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian separately announced that Qatar will release $6 billion of the roughly $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets held there, a development that could serve as a confidence-building measure ahead of Tuesday's negotiations. Iran also resumed scheduled commercial flights to Dubai for the first time since the conflict began in late February, a signal that both sides are seeking to dial back hostilities.

The renewed talks come days after Vice President JD Vance had announced that the two countries had reached a foundation for a lasting peace deal. The Strait of Hormuz remains at the center of tensions, with Iran viewing its ability to threaten the waterway as critical leverage. Senator Bill Cassidy (R-La.) separately criticized Trump's handling of the Iran conflict, accusing the president of treating Congress as "merely an appendage" in his conduct of the war.

Analysts note that ending the now five-month-old conflict remains deeply complicated. Iran's nuclear program and missile arsenal were left intact under the April ceasefire, and reconstruction funding unlocked by that agreement has drawn criticism from hawkish voices on both sides of the aisle who warn that a partial resolution could leave a wounded but still dangerous adversary.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Overturn $5 Million E. Jean Carroll Verdict
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear President Trump's appeal of the jury verdict finding him liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll, leaving intact the $5 million civil award. The court issued a brief, unexplained order denying the petition, which is standard practice when the justices decline to take up a case. The ruling means Carroll is in line to collect the full award.

A unanimous federal jury had found that a preponderance of the evidence supported Carroll's claim that Trump sexually abused her in a Manhattan department store dressing room in the mid-1990s and later defamed her. Trump has consistently denied the allegations, calling them false and politically motivated. He had sought to have the verdict thrown out after years of legal challenges.

The decision is a significant legal setback for the sitting president, closing off a final avenue for overturning the jury's findings through the nation's highest court. Trump's legal team had argued the case should be revisited on procedural and substantive grounds. Carroll's attorneys argued the jury's verdict was well-supported by the evidence and should stand.

The ruling comes as the Supreme Court also prepares to issue opinions this week on birthright citizenship and the president's authority to dismiss the head of the Federal Reserve — two cases with far broader policy implications for the Trump administration.

stories.headline: Five Killed in Shooting at Youth Welfare Centre in Northern Germany
stories.summary:
Five people were killed and several others injured in a shooting at a youth welfare center in Stade, a city of roughly 50,000 people located about 30 kilometers west of Hamburg, German police said Monday. Two people were arrested in connection with the attack, one of whom is considered a suspect. Authorities said there was no further threat to the public.

Police described the incident as involving "homicides with multiple victims" at a youth welfare facility, without providing details on the ages of the victims or a possible motive. Large numbers of emergency personnel were deployed to the scene, and the public was urged to avoid the area while the investigation continued.

The attack is the latest mass shooting incident in Germany, a country that has faced a series of high-profile public violence events in recent years, including the 2024 Magdeburg Christmas market attack that killed six. German authorities have faced ongoing debate over security measures at public facilities and the handling of individuals with mental health histories.

Further details on the identities of the victims, the suspect's background, and the circumstances of the attack were not immediately available. Investigators were expected to provide an update later Monday.

stories.headline: Update: European Heatwave Kills 1,000 Additional in France as Records Fall Across Central Europe
stories.summary:
France's national public health agency reported Sunday that the country experienced at least 1,000 additional deaths during just three days at the peak of its record-breaking heatwave last week. Daily death totals surpassed 1,200 on Wednesday and exceeded 1,400 on each of the two following days, compared to a baseline of roughly 900 to 1,000 deaths per day in the weeks prior. The surge was especially acute in private homes in the Paris region.

The heatwave has now moved eastward, setting all-time national temperature records in multiple countries over the weekend. Germany recorded 41.7°C (107°F) for a third consecutive day, Poland hit a new national high of 40.5°C (104.9°F), and the Czech Republic reached 41.9°C (107.4°F), surpassing its previous record set just the day before. Wildfires broke out in Germany, and Berlin police used water cannons to cool crowds.

The World Health Organization's director-general warned Sunday that Europe is now the fastest-warming continent and must do more to protect its citizens. A rapid attribution study published Friday by the World Weather Attribution consortium concluded the heatwave would have been virtually impossible without climate change and is approximately 200 times more likely today than it was 20 years ago.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes Russian Oil Refinery as Putin Admits Fuel Shortages for First Time
stories.summary:
Ukraine continued its intensified long-range drone campaign against Russian energy infrastructure on Sunday, setting fire to a major oil refinery in Slavyansk-na-Kubani in Russia's Krasnodar region. Regional authorities confirmed falling debris killed one person and wounded another. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strikes hit two oil refineries over the weekend, calling them "long-range sanctions" that reduce resources fueling the Russian war machine.

In a notably candid admission, President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time that Russia faces a "certain deficit" of fuel as a result of Ukrainian strikes. The attacks have caused widespread shortages, long lines at gas stations, and fuel rationing across multiple Russian regions. Western analysts say the campaign has also slowed Russian battlefield advances and increased pressure on Moscow to negotiate.

Putin rejected Ukrainian proposals that were disclosed publicly for the first time Sunday, including an offer to halt deep strikes and to limit fighting to the four regions Russia annexed but never fully captured. He argued the proposals would allow Ukraine to redeploy forces and create negotiating conditions favorable to Kyiv. Putin insisted the strikes have "absolutely no effect" on front-line operations, a claim that his own admission of fuel shortages appeared to undercut.

stories.headline: South Africa Senior Police Intelligence Official Shot in Johannesburg Days Before Corruption Inquiry Appearance
stories.summary:
Maj-Gen Feroz Khan, deputy head of South Africa's crime intelligence division, was shot Sunday evening while driving home in Johannesburg and rushed to hospital for emergency surgery. The shooting occurred just days before Khan was scheduled to appear before the Madlanga Commission, a public inquiry established to investigate alleged infiltration of the police service by organized crime.

Khan was already facing serious legal jeopardy before the shooting. He and two other individuals were arrested last month on charges of illegal dealing in and unlawful possession of precious metals, stemming from a 2021 incident at OR Tambo International Airport. Prosecutors allege Khan instructed officers to release a businessman caught with unwrought gold, and that no legitimate undercover operation existed at the time.

South African police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said in a statement that an investigation is underway but cautioned against speculation about motive, calling it "premature and irresponsible" to link the shooting to Khan's upcoming commission appearance. The Madlanga Commission was created after a senior officer alleged last year that organized crime had penetrated the government at senior levels.

stories.headline: Update: Mother and Newborn Rescued from Venezuela Earthquake Rubble Speak to Media
stories.summary:
Dayana Patino, the Venezuelan mother pulled from the rubble of her collapsed apartment building with her 18-day-old son Juan David, gave her first detailed account of the ordeal Sunday from a clinic in Caracas. She described being thrown through the air when the earthquakes struck, landing in a pit with her left leg trapped under concrete and her temple pressed against a rock, while holding her infant throughout. She said she rationed her energy and screamed only when she heard voices nearby.

Patino said her baby kept her focused on survival. "As long as he was alive, I was going to be alive," she told the BBC, recounting that she repeatedly touched her son's nose in the darkness to confirm he was breathing. Her brother eventually heard her cries and organized a delicate rescue operation that brought both mother and child out of the rubble on Thursday night. Juan David sustained only minor injuries; Patino suffered injuries to both legs.

The rescue became widely shared internationally and the infant has become a symbol of hope amid Venezuela's ongoing disaster response. The country's twin earthquakes have killed at least 1,450 people, with tens of thousands still missing. Authorities have described it as the most severe natural catastrophe in Venezuela's history, and search teams have warned that hopes of finding additional survivors are diminishing.
